analysis.title: Macro Quarterly Q4 2026: Bonds: Normal for Longer
key_insights: UBS AM argues current bond yields look high only against the post-GFC decade of low growth, deleveraging, QE, zero rates and inflation shortfalls. Against longer history they are close to norms, and US 10-year yields are just above their long-term average.

Strong nominal growth, not fiscal concerns, is the main force keeping yields elevated. After the Iran conflict began, investors expected stagflation. The result was reflation: inflation rose, but consumption, AI capex and manufacturing strengthened and earnings expectations rose.
The Atlanta Fed is tracking Q3 GDP growth at 5%, which explains higher equities and higher bond yields together.

Household and corporate leverage are at multi-decade lows after the post-GFC deleveraging. This let the economy absorb the tightest global tightening cycle in decades, the Russia-Ukraine and Iran energy shocks, and rising tariffs without a spending retrenchment.

Yields have risen across most developed markets, in many cases by more than in the US, which weakens the fiscal explanation. Most of the rise in long-term yields is explained by higher policy-rate expectations.

Stock-bond correlations have historically turned positive once inflation moves above roughly 3%. A return to negative or near-zero correlation depends on central banks getting inflation closer to 2%, which UBS AM expects.
Bonds remain a hedge against growth shocks but not inflation shocks. If the outlook for AI investment, consumption or activity deteriorated, lower yields would likely accompany it.

Allocation: still prefers equities to fixed income, but the duration selloff makes government bonds more attractive than at any point in much of the past decade. It favors adding sovereign duration on dips, especially outside the US, and a more structural role for commodities and gold as inflation diversifiers.

Asset class views as of 23 Sep 2026 (3-12 month horizon): overweight global equities, with EM and Japan preferred over Europe and Switzerland. US neutral, Europe underweight (weaker earnings growth, elevated gas prices) except European banks, which it likes.

Rates: overweight global government bonds and gilts, neutral on US Treasuries, Bunds, JGBs and Swiss bonds. Prefers duration in the UK (weaker labor market) and Australia (weaker housing market). The US rates market is pricing a tightening cycle of close to 5 hikes, which may not materialize if inflation falls.

Credit is neutral across global, IG, HY and EM hard-currency debt. Heavy hyperscaler and AI-related IG supply should stop spreads narrowing further, and HY spreads are expected to stay tight. It is overweight EM local-currency debt for selective carry.

FX: neutral USD, EUR and JPY, underweight CHF as a funder, overweight high-carry EM currencies including ZAR. Commodities: overweight gold on central bank buying led by China, and Brent seen in a USD 80 to 120 range while the US-Iran conflict persists.

sector_views.rationale: Should benefit from strong earnings and elevated rates, even though UBS AM is underweight European equities overall.
Tech continues to lead US earnings, and the MSCI EM index is heavily weighted toward North Asian tech giants that benefit from the AI capex cycle.

earnings_insights: UBS AM expects US earnings to remain strong with nominal GDP elevated, and says earnings growth is broadening beyond tech. Earnings are strong across most EM regions and Japan screens well on EPS revisions. European earnings growth is weaker than in other regions.

UBS AM's range while the US-Iran conflict persists, which keeps energy inflation and EM central bank spillover risks live.

trade_ideas.description: Add sovereign duration on dips, particularly outside the US, with preference for UK gilts and Australian government bonds
trade_ideas.rationale: Higher starting yields give a better cushion, and growth is vulnerable in the UK labor market and Australian housing market.
trade_ideas.risk: Stickier inflation, where bonds would not hedge and stock-bond correlation stays positive.

trade_ideas.description: Structural allocation to gold and commodities as inflation diversifiers; overweight gold
trade_ideas.rationale: They have historically performed well during inflation surprises and central banks, led by China, are strong buyers.
trade_ideas.risk: Higher real yields, which gold has so far weathered.

trade_ideas.description: Overweight high-carry EM currencies including ZAR, underweight CHF as a funding currency
trade_ideas.rationale: High real interest rates amid strong manufacturing growth, positive risk sentiment and rising commodity prices; CHF has low yields and expensive valuation.

risk_factors: Inflation surprises, which hurt both stocks and bonds when inflation is above about 3%.
A reassessment of AI investment, consumption or broader activity.
Elevated European natural gas prices and renewed energy price increases threatening the European recovery.
Heavy hyperscaler and AI-related IG issuance limiting spread tightening.
Inflation spillovers from the Iran conflict forcing EM central banks to react.
US tightening of close to 5 hikes priced, which may not materialize if inflation falls.
charts_described: Exhibit 4 decomposes the year-to-date change in 10-year government bond yields across major developed markets, as of 22 September 2026, with most of the increase explained by higher policy-rate expectations.
vol_and_positioning: UBS AM expects HY credit spreads to stay tight and volatility to stay low, consistent with mid-cycle dynamics.
Stock-bond correlations are positive in the current above-3% inflation regime, which reduces bonds' hedging value in inflation shocks.
geopolitical: Iran conflict: expected to lift inflation and weaken growth, but growth strengthened. The US-Iran conflict persists, supporting Brent at USD 80 to 120 and spilling inflation into EM central banks.
Russia-Ukraine and Iran energy shocks were absorbed by the economy.
Rising tariffs and growing trade restrictions were absorbed without a spending retrenchment.

tension_points.bull_case: Bonds still protect against growth shocks, and higher starting yields give a better cushion than in the post-GFC period. Duration is attractive on dips, especially outside the US.
tension_points.bear_case: With inflation above about 3%, stock-bond correlations turn positive and bonds come under pressure during inflation surprises.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Inflation staying above roughly 3% would keep stock-bond correlations positive; a return of inflation toward 2% targets would restore negative or near-zero correlation.

theme_stances.key_argument: Yields look high only against the abnormal post-GFC decade and are close to historical norms.
theme_stances.evidence: the post-GFC era was the exception, not the rule

theme_stances.key_argument: The duration selloff makes government bonds more attractive, with UK and Australia growth most vulnerable.
theme_stances.evidence: We favor adding sovereign duration on dips, particularly in markets outside the United States.

theme_stances.key_argument: Growth strengthened after the Iran conflict began alongside higher inflation, so the result was reflation.
theme_stances.evidence: many investors predicted stagflation; instead, we got reflation.
